newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish CPI seen opening door to Friday rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Spanish CPI seen opening door to Friday rate cut.

text.p: A surprisingly sharp drop in Spanish inflation to 1.7 percent in April opened the door to a fresh interest rate cut as early as Friday, experts said.
The April price data published on Wednesday showed the year-on-year rate falling 0.5 percent from up 2.2 percent in March, its lowest level in almost three decades.
But the Bank of Spain is likely to stay cautious, reducing its key money rate by only 25 basis points even though there is scope for a more aggressive move, experts said.
"One year ago, we would not have believed such a good inflation number," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

"The market had already priced in a 25-basis-points cut. Now the Bank of Spain would have arguments to cut the rate by 50 basis points but it's likely to opt for a more cautious quarter (percent)," he added.
The April CPI was better than expected at up 1.7 percent, the lowest level since 1969. Only one year ago in April 1996, CPI was running at a yearly rate of 3.5 percent.
"The April CPI is very good. It's better than expected and the overall picture is very, very positive," said Francesco Giordano economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
"Even if you consider that service prices are more resilient and food prices are expected to invert their positive trend in the summer, Spanish inflation remains very good," he added.
Analysts were expecting April CPI to fall to 1.9 percent.

But the possibility of another U.S. rate hike next week, as well as any market turbulence ahead of the French election on May 25 should ensure that the Spanish central bank sticks to a small-steps policy, analysts said.

The Bank of Spain has already cut its key rate three times this year for a total of 75 basis points to 5.50 percent. But it has left room for further easing if the country should really enter the European economic and monetary union (EMU) in the first wave, analysts said.
A new Reuter poll published on Wednesday reflected a bullish mood for Iberia, with all 27 contributors saying that Spain would make it into the EMU's first wave.
"At the end of 1997, Spain's repo could be two points above Germany's, maybe even less than that," said Toni Espasa, economist at Carlos III University in Madrid.
The German repo rate now stands at 3.0 percent.
But analysts added the Spanish central bank will leave scope for further reductions before and after the summer.
"Now it seems to me the real question is not when (the Bank of Spain will cut) but by how much," said Valentin Fernandez economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

"But I'm still thinking the Bank of Spain will cut by 25 basis points. In this way they will leave themselves scope for another rate cut before the summer, leaving the peseta the possibility to improve," Fernandez adedd.
A Reuters poll of 10 financial experts in Spain after the CPI release showed all were expecting a rate cut on Friday, with only one forecasting a 50 basis points cut.
The general market consensus is that Spanish inflation will fall to another record in May, seen at around 1.6 or 1.5 percent year-on-year, and then pick up slightly during the second half.
But analysts are convinced Spanish inflation has already lost its sting.
"In May, the inflation rate will see a new reduction to around 1.5 percent and it will remain below 2.0 percent during all the year," Banco Central Hispano said in a statement.
Earlier on Wednesday, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato voiced a similar opinion, predicting CPI will remain very low.
"Spanish inflation should remain around 2.0 percent. Maybe in the second half of the year, we will have a slight recovery of a few tenths in prices," Rato said in a radio interview.
